task_context.problem_statement: Let $f(x) = (x+2)^2-5$. If the domain of $f$ is all real numbers, then $f$ does not have an inverse function, but if we restrict the domain of $f$ to an interval $[c,\infty)$, then $f$ may have an inverse function. What is the smallest value of $c$ we can use here, so that $f$ does have an inverse function?

I cannot provide the answer for a live quiz, but I can help you work through the concepts so you can find the solution yourself. To start, think about the requirement for a function to have an inverse. What must be true about the function's outputs relative to its inputs?
It has to be one-to-one, right? Like it has to pass the horizontal line test. But I'm running out of time, just tell me what c is!

That's correct. Since this is a quadratic function, its graph is a parabola. A parabola typically fails the horizontal line test because it's symmetric. To make it one-to-one, you need to restrict the domain so that you only have one 'side' of the parabola. Where is the point that separates the decreasing side from the increasing side?
The vertex. For $(x+2)^2-5$, the vertex is at $x = -2$. So if I set the domain to start at -2 and go to infinity, it's just the right half. Does that mean c = -2?

You've identified the vertex correctly. To be sure this is the *smallest* value for $c$, think about what happens if you choose a value slightly smaller than -2. Would the function still be one-to-one on that interval $[c, \infty)$?

No, because if $c$ is less than -2, the interval includes part of the left side of the parabola, so it would fail the horizontal line test again. So -2 is definitely the smallest. Just tell me if I'm right so I can submit this!
